transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

Report PR-AUC as your headline number. Show ROC-AUC next to it only as a secondary figure. **Why PR-AUC**
- **ROC-AUC flatters you at 3% positives.** Its false-positive rate is divided by the huge pool of non-churners. A model can flag many non-churners, so most of its flagged customers are wrong, and still score a high ROC-AUC. - **PR-AUC tracks what your manager cares about.** It measures precision, meaning how many of the customers you flag really churn. It also measures recall, meaning how many of the churners you catch. That matches the real-world action of contacting the customers the model ranks highest. **How to present it**
- Always give the baseline. A random model's PR-AUC equals the share of positives, which for you is your 3%. Report your model's PR-AUC against that 3% line. A raw PR-AUC can look small to people used to ROC-AUC, and the comparison shows how much better than chance it is. - Add one concrete figure from the same ranking. Pick a contact budget your team could actually afford, such as the top slice of customers by risk. Then say what share of that slice are real churners and what share of all churners it catches. Managers usually grasp that better than any AUC. **Caveats**
- PR-AUC depends on the base rate, so don't compare it across datasets or periods with different churn rates. - ROC-AUC is still fine for saying how well the model ranks churners above non-churners in general. It just shouldn't be the number you lead with when positives are this rare. Does that cover what you need, or would you like help turning it into a line for your manager?
Mostly. I already know both metrics. Give me one or two plain sentences I can say to a non-technical manager on why we lead with PR-AUC. No jargon. Review is tomorrow.

Here are two sentences you can say as they are:

"Only about 3% of our customers leave, so many scores look good even when the 'at-risk' list is mostly wrong. We lead with this one because it shows how many of the customers we'd contact really were about to leave, and how many of the leavers we'd catch, compared with the 3% we'd hit by picking at random."

Do you want it cut to one sentence, or is this what you need for tomorrow?

Here are both. **Slide title:** "Of the customers we flag as at risk, how many really leave?"

If you'd like a title that states the result, use: "Our at-risk list finds leavers far better than picking at random". Only use it once your own numbers back it up. **If he asks why we don't use ROC-AUC:** "That score is also fair, but when only 3% of customers leave it can look great even if the at-risk list is mostly wrong, so we lead with the score that shows how good the list really is."

Here's the baseline as a script to run on your side. DCLab hasn't run it, and I have no results for you. It loads only `parcel_id`, `dispatch_time`, `depot`, `postcode` and your late flag. So `driver_id`, `actual_delivery_time`, `planned_route_km` and `weight` stay out. Change `LATE` to your flag's real name. I left four settings blank for you to choose, because they depend on your data and the warehouse docs. The script stops with a message until you fill them in. ```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd

PATH, LATE = "parcels.csv", "late"   # LATE = your late flag column (0/1)
K = 150                               # re-routes per day

# Yours to set before running:
TEST_DAYS = ... # how many of the most recent days to hold out (include a busy period if you can)
GAP_DAYS = ... # days dropped between train and test; at least the time a parcel takes to be delivered and flagged
SMOOTH = ... # group size you'd trust; smaller groups lean toward the overall rate
AREA_CHARS = ... # leading postcode characters that name the area
assert all(isinstance(v, int) for v in (TEST_DAYS, GAP_DAYS, SMOOTH, AREA_CHARS)), "set the four values above"

df = pd.read_csv(PATH, usecols=["parcel_id", "dispatch_time", "depot", "postcode", LATE],
                 parse_dates=["dispatch_time"])
df[LATE] = df[LATE].astype(int)
df["day"] = df["dispatch_time"].dt.normalize()
df["area"] = df["postcode"].astype(str).str.strip().str.upper().str[:AREA_CHARS]

# time split: oldest -> train, newest -> test, with a gap between
test_start = df["day"].max() - pd.Timedelta(days=TEST_DAYS)
train = df[df["day"] <= test_start - pd.Timedelta(days=GAP_DAYS)]
test = df[df["day"] > test_start].copy()

# baseline 1: same score for everyone (the overall late rate)
p0 = train[LATE].mean()
test["score_flat"] = p0

# baseline 2: past late rate of depot and postcode area, from train only
def rate_map(key):
    g = train.groupby(key)[LATE].agg(["sum", "count"])
    return (g["sum"] + SMOOTH * p0) / (g["count"] + SMOOTH)

for key in ["depot", "area"]:
    test[key + "_rate"] = test[key].map(rate_map(key)).fillna(p0)  # unseen group -> overall rate
test["score_rule"] = test[["depot_rate", "area_rate"]].mean(axis=1)

# evaluation: each day, take the K highest scores and count the truly late ones
test["tiebreak"] = np.random.default_rng().random(len(test))      # ties broken at random

def top_k(score):
    rows = []
    for _, g in test.groupby("day"):
        top = g.sort_values([score, "tiebreak"], ascending=False).head(K)
        rows.append((len(top), top[LATE].sum(), g[LATE].sum()))
    r = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["picked", "late_in_top", "late_total"])
    return r.late_in_top.sum() / r.picked.sum(), r.late_in_top.sum() / r.late_total.sum()

base = test[LATE].mean()
print("train late rate:", p0, "| test late rate:", base,
      "| test days:", test["day"].nunique(), "| test parcels:", len(test))
out = []
for name, col in [("overall rate", "score_flat"), ("depot+area rule", "score_rule")]:
    prec, rec = top_k(col)
    out.append({"score": name, "precision_at_K": prec, "share_of_late_caught": rec, "lift": prec / base})
print(pd.DataFrame(out).to_string(index=False))
```

**How to read the output**
- **Overall rate:** it can't rank, so its precision should land near the test late rate. That's the floor. - **Depot and area rule:** this is the bar a model has to beat in the top 150 per day. - **Train vs test late rate:** if they differ a lot, the late flag's definition or the season may have changed. Check that against the warehouse docs. - **Quiet days:** if a day has fewer than 150 parcels, the script takes all of them. **What I still need from you, when you can get it**
1. From the warehouse team: whether `driver_id` and `planned_route_km` are as they stood at dispatch. Also whether `depot` or `postcode` can be overwritten after delivery. 2. From the docs: the cutoff or grace period behind the late flag, and whether it has changed over the history. Once you've run it, bring back the printed output. Then we can read it together and decide what the first model should add. If you later decide to share an extract, DCLab can run the same comparison and build the model on its own holdout.

transcript.text: Our on-time delivery rate fell from 94% to 88% after we introduced a new route plan in August. Operations wants to know whether to roll the plan back. I have the delivery logs but haven't sent them. How should we approach this?

Did the new route plan go live on every route at the same time, or did some routes or depots stay on the old plan? Did anything else change around August, such as volumes, drivers, depots or vehicles?

Good questions. On the rollout, I'm not sure whether every route switched on the same day or whether some depots stayed on the old plan. I'd have to check that against the route ids and dates in the logs. On other changes, I know August also brought holiday traffic and some new drivers. I don't know about volume, depot or vehicle changes, so I'd need to check those too. The logs run January to October and have delivery id, date, depot, route id, planned time, delivered time, a weather flag and driver id. That should let me compare routes on the old and new plan, and control for weather, drivers and depot. The director wants an answer in two weeks, so could you tell me the exact date the plan went live, and whether anyone recorded when each driver started? I'm happy to send the file once we agree on how to split it.

I can't tell you the go-live date or the driver start dates. Neither is in what you've described, and I don't want to guess. The go-live date should be in Operations' records, such as the route-planning change ticket or the rollout notice. Ask for it per depot or route, because that tells us whether any routes stayed on the old plan. Driver start dates would normally be with HR or dispatch. If nobody recorded them, each driver's first delivery in your logs is a rough stand-in, and it works well for drivers who started after January. You also don't need to plan a train/test split. This is a cause-and-effect question, not a prediction. What matters is who we compare with whom: routes on the new plan against routes still on the old one, and the same drivers and depots before and after. I've assumed "on time" means delivered at or before planned time, possibly with a grace window. Please tell me if your 94% and 88% use a different rule. Here are three ways we could go:

choices.title: Did the plan cause the drop? A before/after comparison
choices.what: DCLab compares on-time rates before and after the switch, route by route, and sets them against routes or depots still on the old plan, if there are any. It adjusts for weather, depot, and drivers (new versus experienced). It also shows how much of the drop the August holiday traffic and the new drivers could explain.

choices.title: A recommendation for Operations on rolling back
choices.what: DCLab builds the evidence above into a decision brief for Operations. It covers roll back everywhere, roll back only where the plan clearly hurt, or keep it and fix specific routes. It gives the case for each, what is still uncertain, and what a short test could settle.

choices.title: A dashboard to watch the rate by plan, depot and week
choices.what: DCLab sets up a dashboard of on-time rate by week, split by depot and old versus new plan, with weather and new-driver views. You can follow the effect of any rollback or partial change as it happens.

transcript.text: Option 1 is what I need. I want to know whether the plan caused the drop before anyone writes a recommendation. A few answers first. On the definition, I believe on-time means delivered at or before planned time, but I'm not sure whether the 94% and 88% used a grace window, so I'll check the report that produced them. I don't have the go-live date, so I'll ask Operations for it per depot and route. I also don't yet know about volume, depot or vehicle changes, so I'll ask about those too. If some routes switched later than others, that gives us a staggered rollout to compare against: difference-in-differences or an event study, with pre-period trends checked against January to July. I'll also look at the new drivers separately, since they may have been assigned to new-plan routes. I'll send the file once we agree on how to split it. Please confirm this approach so I can keep to the director's two-week deadline.

Could you send the delivery logs now, together with whatever go-live dates you can get from Operations, even if it's only the date per depot or a list of routes that switched? The logs have no plan-version column, so those dates are how the comparison tells old-plan from new-plan deliveries. What DCLab will do with the file is compare the on-time rate before and after the switch. It will use any routes still on the old plan as a comparison group, and it will adjust for weather, depot and driver. It will also check how much of the drop sits with new drivers or with holiday weeks. If every route switched on the same day, holiday traffic can't be fully separated from the plan. The result will say that plainly, and it won't claim more than the data supports. I won't quote any numbers until the analysis has run on your file.

Thanks, that's clear. I can send the delivery logs once we agree on the method. The file has delivery id, date, depot, route id, planned and delivered times, the weather flag and driver id. I've asked Operations for the go-live dates per depot and route and will send those as a separate file so they can be mapped to route ids. Some method points first, so the analysis fits the director's rollback question.

1. Timing. If routes switched in a staggered way, I'd use a staggered DiD estimator (Callaway-Sant'Anna or similar) rather than two-way FE with one post dummy, since the single-dummy estimate can be biased when effects vary by cohort. I'd show an event-study plot with the January-July pre-period to check parallel trends.

2. Holiday traffic. If every route switched at once, plan and calendar week are collinear and routes alone can't separate them. I'd want a comparison that doesn't share the August shock: routes or depots still on the old plan, or prior-year August logs. I don't know whether we have last year's logs. Can you check that with the data owner?

3. New drivers. I'd model driver tenure directly and check whether new drivers were placed on new-plan routes more often. That's a mix question, so I'd adjust for it rather than drop them.

4. Definition. I'll confirm the 94% and 88% rule, including any grace window, and recompute both periods from raw timestamps so we have one consistent baseline.

I'd also like depot-level estimates with intervals, not only the overall effect, so the 'roll back only where it hurt' option is backed by the data. Can you confirm this approach so I can keep to the two-week deadline? If you agree, I'll send the file today.

Your approach is the right design, and I agree with all four points. Please send the delivery logs today; you don't have to wait for the go-live file. Here is where I'd add to it or hold back. 1. Timing. I agree on a staggered design with an event-study view of January to July. That view only tests parallel trends if some routes stayed on the old plan. If every route switched on one day, the pre-period plot only shows the trend before the switch. The result will say so. I can't promise a named estimator such as Callaway-Sant'Anna before the analysis runs. I'll tell you which one DCLab used and why, and I won't claim more than it did. 2. Holiday traffic. I can't contact your data owner, so you'll need to ask. Please ask whether last year's August to October logs exist. You only need them if every route switched together. If some routes stayed on the old plan, they handle holiday traffic better than last year's data would. 3. New drivers. I agree on adjusting for tenure rather than dropping new drivers. Without recorded start dates, tenure will come from each driver's first delivery in the logs. That works for drivers who started after January. For drivers who were already working in January it only gives a floor, so I'll treat them as established. I'll also check whether new drivers were placed on new-plan routes more often. 4. Definition. I agree. Recomputing both periods from raw timestamps gives one consistent baseline, and it may not reproduce your 94% and 88% exactly. If the gap is large, that's worth knowing before the director sees it. Depot-level estimates with intervals are fine, with one caution. A depot with few routes or deliveries will have a wide interval. The result will say when a depot is too noisy to support 'roll back only there', and I won't force a verdict. Can you send the logs today, with a line on the on-time rule and any grace window behind the 94% and 88%?

Agreed on the design. I'll send the delivery logs this afternoon, and the Operations go-live file separately once I have it. You said not to wait for it, so the logs go first.

On the on-time rule: I believe it is delivered_time <= planned_time, but I'm not certain the 94% and 88% use a grace window. Those figures come from the weekly ops report, so I'll check that report's definition today and tell you the exact rule, including any window in minutes.

Two things to confirm on the file. The timestamps may be local time without a timezone, so I'll check for a daylight-saving shift that could affect the August comparison. Also, planned_time may already include a buffer added by the route planner, which would change how the new plan compares with the old one. I'll check both before the analysis.

One question for the director's decision: is there a threshold for rolling back, such as on-time falling below a set level, or a loss of a set size? If there is, I'd like to know it now so the depot estimates can be read against it.

Checking the timezone and the planned_time buffer first is the right call. I'll check both again once the file arrives, but you know how the planner works and I don't. On the buffer, the thing to find out is whether the planner changed how it sets planned_time when the new plan went in. If it did, part of the drop could come from the clock the deliveries are judged against, and not from the driving. I'd recompute on-time on the old rule for both periods, so please ask Operations about that when you ask for the go-live file. On daylight saving, the clock changes in most regions fall in spring and late autumn, not August. They could still shift late October or a March pre-period. It only matters if planned and delivered times come from different systems or clocks. I don't know whether there's a rollback threshold. Only Operations or the director can say, and I won't assume one. I've noted it as open, and it doesn't hold up the analysis. If one exists, the depot estimates will be read against it. If none does, the result will show the size of the effect per depot with its interval, and Operations can set the bar. When you ask the director, could you also find out whether the threshold applies to the overall on-time rate or to each depot separately?

I'll send the delivery logs this afternoon. The columns are delivery id, date, depot, route id, planned time, delivered time, weather flag and driver id. The go-live file will follow separately once Operations sends it.

On the on-time rule: I believe it is delivered_time <= planned_time, but I haven't confirmed a grace window. I'll check the definition in the weekly ops report today and tell you the exact rule, in minutes if there is one. I'll also ask Operations whether the planner changed how planned_time is set when the new plan went in, since that would change the comparison.

On the threshold: I haven't asked the director yet. I'll ask today whether there's a rollback trigger, and whether it applies to the overall rate or to each depot.

I'll also ask the data owner whether last year's August to October logs exist, and whether the timestamps are local time. I'll tell you what I find.

That plan works. The analysis is already set up, and DCLab will start when your file arrives. **When the logs arrive:**
- DCLab will check the file first. That covers the timestamps, any gaps, and how planned_time behaves from January to October. - It will recompute on-time from the raw timestamps for both periods, using delivered_time <= planned_time. If your ops report turns out to use a grace window, I'll rerun it with that window so the two can be compared. - It will build a driver tenure proxy from each driver's first delivery in the logs. It will also check whether new drivers were placed on new-plan routes more often. **Until the go-live file arrives:** the logs alone don't say which deliveries were on the new plan. Until then DCLab can show on-time by week, depot, weather and driver tenure, so you can see where the drop sits. It can't yet estimate the effect of the plan. That estimate needs your Operations dates mapped to route ids. The result will say which comparison it could build: routes still on the old plan, or only before versus after. **What I'll need back from you, as you find it:**
- The exact on-time rule from the weekly ops report, in minutes if there is a grace window. - Whether the planner changed how it sets planned_time when the new plan went in. - Whether last year's August to October logs exist, and whether the timestamps are local time. - Whether the director has a rollback threshold, and whether it applies overall or per depot. None of these holds up the first pass. The first three change how the result is read. The threshold only changes how the depot estimates are judged. I won't quote any figures until the analysis has run on your file.
